n0001.title: A Ruliology of Bugs
n0001.gist: Because simple programs already harbor computational irreducibility, bugs are an inevitable, structural feature of computation, not mere human error.
n0001.question: Why do bugs exist — what makes them a fundamental, unavoidable feature of computation rather than just mistakes? (a theory built from simple examples)

n0002.title: My Program Did the Wrong Thing!
n0002.gist: Bugs arise because programs can be computationally irreducible, meaning even very simple code can behave in ways no simple mental model can foresee.
n0002.question: What is a bug, fundamentally — can there be a general theory of why programs surprise us? (an opening argument)

n0003.title: Framing the question
n0003.gist: The essay sets out to find a scientific theory of bugs, arguing that computational irreducibility explains why even AI-assisted testing cannot fully foresee program behavior.

n0007.title: Ruliology and expectations
n0007.gist: Studying simple programs with ruliology's methods reveals why what we expect a program to do can diverge from what it actually computes, once its process outruns our mental model.

n0013.title: Irreducibility as the source
n0013.gist: The Principle of Computational Equivalence implies that even simple-looking programs can compute in sophisticated, unforeseeable ways, which is what produces what we call bugs.

n0016.title: Bugs in Turing Machines
n0016.gist: Minimal Turing machines meant to add one to a number often work correctly for many inputs before suddenly failing at a specific, sometimes very distant, value.
n0016.question: Bugs in Turing machines — how far must you test a simple machine before a hidden flaw appears? (worked examples)

n0017.title: A first glitching machine
n0017.gist: A simple 3-state Turing machine meant to compute n+1 works correctly for small inputs but suddenly fails at n=7, producing recurring glitches at every number ending in 111 in binary.

n0029.title: How far until a bug appears
n0029.gist: Among thousands of small machines that compute n+1 correctly, some hide their first error until surprisingly large inputs, including one whose bug first appears only at n=15.

n0044.title: Larger machines, later bugs
n0044.gist: Among millions of 4-state machines that successfully compute n+1, some pass every test up to n=62 before failing, showing bugs can be pushed arbitrarily far from view by adding more states.

n0052.title: What Counts as a Bug?
n0052.gist: Whether something counts as a bug depends entirely on the specification chosen to judge it, whether that specification restates expected behavior or forbids certain outcomes like infinite loops.
n0052.question: What counts as a bug — what makes some unexpected behavior a bug rather than just what the program does? (several specification types)

n0053.title: Specifications define bugs
n0053.gist: A program only has a bug relative to some simpler specification of what it should do, since judged against itself a program always just does what it does.

n0057.title: Comparing equivalent programs
n0057.gist: Two Turing machines that appear to compute the same function can quietly diverge at a specific input, like n=27, with the resulting mismatches following a surprisingly complicated pattern.

n0064.title: Constraints as specifications
n0064.gist: Machines can be specified by what they must avoid, such as unbounded memory use, infinite loops, or odd outputs, yet seemingly well-behaved machines still eventually violate each such constraint.

n0080.title: A Cellular Automaton Example
n0080.gist: Cellular automata built to double an input block of cells illustrate the same pattern as Turing machines: many rules work correctly for a long stretch of inputs before suddenly failing.
n0080.question: Cellular automata — does the same bug pattern seen in Turing machines also show up here? (several doubling-rule examples)

n0094.title: Can One Tell If There's Going to Be a Bug?
n0094.gist: Visual simplicity alone can prove a cellular automaton has no bugs, and even some visually complex ones can be proven bug-free by tracking a bounding edge and an interior effective rule.
n0094.question: Predicting bugs in advance — can you tell from a cellular automaton's look whether it will ever fail? (a worked proof)
n0094.sourceHeading: Can One Tell If There's Going to Be a Bug?

n0095.title: Visual obviousness and its limits
n0095.gist: Some cellular automata are visually simple enough to trust completely, but others that look similarly contained still show random-looking fluctuations with no obvious guarantee against failure.

n0115.title: A proof from the pattern's edge
n0115.gist: Tracking the boundary of a complex-looking pattern and reducing its interior to a simpler effective rule shows that it can never expand or stall, proving the doubling process never has bugs.

n0130.title: But What about Formal Proofs?
n0130.gist: Turing machine behavior can sometimes be formally proved correct using symbolic axioms and induction, but for machines with real bugs no such proof exists because the claim is simply false.
n0130.question: Formal proofs — can we mathematically guarantee a program has no bugs, and what happens when it does have one? (several proof examples)

n0131.title: Setting up a symbolic proof
n0131.gist: Representing a Turing machine's tape as symbolic expressions with algebraic axioms lets one state precisely, in finite symbolic form, what it would mean for the machine to always compute n+1.

n0158.title: Proving correctness by induction
n0158.gist: Using automated equational proof search and mathematical induction, one can derive a finite proof that a simple machine computes n+1 for every input, collapsing infinitely many cases into one argument.

n0167.title: Why buggy machines resist proof
n0167.gist: Building the space of possible proof steps as a multiway graph shows that a correct machine's proof can be found within it, while a buggy machine's false claim can never be reached no matter how far one searches.

n0181.title: Computational Irreducibility and Bugs
n0181.gist: Bugs trace back to computational irreducibility: since useful programs must have unforeseeable behavior, bounded checking can never guarantee the absence of surprises.
n0181.question: Why can't we just avoid bugs by using foreseeable programs? (an argument from necessity)

n0182.title: Irreducibility is unavoidable
n0182.gist: Because the Principle of Computational Equivalence makes computational irreducibility ubiquitous, no bounded amount of checking can ever guarantee a program free of unexpected, bug-like behavior.

n0189.title: Pockets of predictability
n0189.gist: A useful program must contain some irreducibility, yet within it there remain pockets of computational reducibility where certain properties can still be reliably guaranteed, as the earlier proofs showed.

n0194.title: Did I Test Enough Cases?
n0194.gist: Ordinary scientific induction fails in ruliology because computational irreducibility means patterns observed in many test cases can still break without warning, making bug density effectively unbounded.
n0194.question: Testing programs — can repeated successful tests ever justify trusting a pattern will always hold? (no, with reasoning)
n0194.sourceHeading: Did I Test Enough Cases? The Failure of Ruliological Induction

n0195.title: Induction breaks down
n0195.gist: Scientific induction assumes repeated patterns will persist, but computational irreducibility guarantees that ruliological systems can always produce bug-like surprises that defy any inferred law.

n0201.title: Sampling and bug density
n0201.gist: Whether random testing finds bugs depends on whether the randomness is strong enough to reach every special case, and on how astronomically rare the bugs are, a rarity that can be unbounded like the busy beaver problem.

n0208.title: Some Typical Ruliological Surprises
n0208.gist: Decades of exploring simple rules repeatedly show behavior erupting unexpectedly after vast numbers of steps or inputs, confirming that surprise is the rule rather than the exception in the computational universe.
n0208.question: Ruliological surprises — how often and how dramatically do simple systems defy expectation? (several concrete examples)

n0209.title: Early surprises: rule 30 and beyond
n0209.gist: Early ruliological exploration found that enumerating simple cellular automata and Turing machines, nearly all behaving regularly, eventually reveals outliers like rule 30 that produce unexpected complexity.

n0216.title: Surprises from changing inputs
n0216.gist: A single cellular automaton rule can behave consistently across many starting inputs, yet still produce a wholly different and unpredictable pattern at a specific, far-off input value.

n0225.title: Surprises in halting and growth
n0225.gist: Systems that appear to grow forever, loop endlessly, or stay symmetric can abruptly halt, sprout new structure, or hit an impassable dead end after millions of steps, showing irreducibility in action.

n0243.title: Mathematical "Bugs"
n0243.gist: Mathematics can contain its own ruliology-style bugs in the form of astronomically distant counterexamples, but mainstream pure mathematics mostly avoids them by focusing on human-understandable structures.
n0243.question: Mathematical bugs — do mathematical hypotheses face the same kind of hidden counterexample as buggy programs? (several number-theory examples)

n0244.title: Counterexamples found astronomically far out
n0244.gist: Patterns that hold for huge numbers of tested cases in polynomial factorization and prime counting can still reverse at astronomically distant points, revealing hidden counterexamples to tempting hypotheses.

n0255.title: Why mathematics mostly avoids this
n0255.gist: Gödel's theorem shows mathematics is in principle exposed to the same irreducibility as ruliology, but ordinary pure mathematics sidesteps this by favoring human-graspable structures over exhaustive computation.

n0259.title: Experimental mathematics as exception
n0259.gist: When mathematics is pursued experimentally, testing structures the way ruliology tests rules, it becomes just as exposed to computational irreducibility and its accompanying surprises as any other computation.

n0261.title: Bugs in Practice
n0261.gist: Avoiding bugs in practice means designing languages whose primitives match human intent and finding ways to visually see inside a computation, though irreducibility always leaves some risk, especially in opaque systems like neural networks.
n0261.question: Avoiding bugs in practice — what can programmers actually do to reduce, if not eliminate, bugs? (a recommendation)

n0262.title: Language design as defense
n0262.gist: Since fully understanding a program's behavior would make running it pointless, the best defense against bugs is a well-designed language whose primitives match what humans actually intend to compute.

n0271.title: Seeing inside a computation
n0271.gist: Visualizing a program's full behavior, easiest for cellular automata and Turing machines and harder for ordinary software, can give genuine confidence that a system always does the right thing without bugs.

n0276.title: Deep bugs and AI systems
n0276.gist: Beyond ordinary human coding slips lie deeper bugs rooted in computation itself, which also afflict neural networks, whose trained, often incomprehensible internals make unexpected behavior essentially unavoidable.

n0280.title: Bugs as scientific discovery
n0280.gist: Allowing bugs can let a low-level program be shorter, and what engineering treats as failure, science can treat as discovery, since ruliology's progress largely consists of a long sequence of such unexpected findings.

n0283.title: Thanks
n0283.gist: The author credits Wolfram Institute colleagues and the decades-long Wolfram quality assurance team whose handling of hundreds of thousands of bugs shaped his intuition for the phenomenon.
